title: The calico printer
hook: Namdev, a cloth-printer and devotee of Maharashtra, sings with his trade's own tools: the measuring yard, the scissors, the dye

segments.voice: Yesterday, nimrata: Farid's grass on the path, cut and trampled and growing back. Your line was humble to the end.

A wooden block, carved with a pattern. A tray of dye. A length of plain cotton laid flat on a table. Press, lift, move along, press again, until the cloth is covered in flowers. That's calico printing by hand, and tradition says it was the family trade of Namdev, a devotee from Maharashtra, far to the south of the Punjab. His hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in one of them he prays with the tools still in his hands.
screen: `A BLOCK, A DYE, A LENGTH OF CLOTH.` → `NAMDEV OF MAHARASHTRA.` → `PRAYING WITH THE TOOLS IN HAND.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, on Ang 485. In paraphrase: my mind is the measuring yard, and my tongue is the scissors. I measure and measure, and cut away the noose of death. What do I care about caste, what do I care about lineage? I repeat the Lord's Name day and night. I dye what is to be dyed, I sew what is to be sewn, and without the Name I can't live for even a moment. Every tool on the table becomes a way of remembering. The yard is the mind, taking the measure of things. The tongue that says the Name is the scissors, cutting what binds him. The dye vat and the needle stay in use, and the Name runs through all of it. The second turn: right in the middle of that workshop, Namdev asks what caste and lineage have to do with any of this. Some people of his time counted a printer of cloth as low. Namdev doesn't argue the ranking. He walks past it, because the Name doesn't ask what family you came from. The third turn is the Sikh book that keeps this hymn. The Gurus taught kirat karni, earning by honest work, and naam japna, remembering the Name. Namdev's workshop holds both in one room. He isn't a monk who left the table. He's a craftsman who made the table holy. A prayer here doesn't need new words. It can be the old motions of your day, done with the One in mind.
screen: `MY MIND THE YARD, MY TONGUE THE SCISSORS.` · `WHAT DO I CARE ABOUT CASTE?` · `DYEING AND SEWING, WITH THE NAME.` · `WORK AND REMEMBRANCE, ONE ROOM.` · then, large: `A PRINTER'S PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Press a thumb in ink or coffee on a scrap of paper, or use a stamp, a cut potato, a leaf: press, lift, press again, slowly, one breath for each press, not aiming for pretty. If you can't make a mark where you are, press your thumb gently into your palm instead. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each press.
Chhipa. The calico printer's trade tradition gives to Namdev, who prays with the tools still in his hands: the yard, the scissors, the dye.
Your line: a printer's prayer. The tools can stay in your hands. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Namdev's hymns as gurbani, and his picture of praying through ordinary work is often linked to the Sikh ideals of kirat karni, honest work, and naam japna, remembering the Name.
